utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Madam Registrar, would you call the case, place.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is IT-98-29-PT, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to the interpreters, to the technical booth, and good afternoon, once again, to the voice that I've been hearing all afternoon. I hope you're still in a position to be able to work, that you're not too tired, speaking to the French interpreter. Let me turn to the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Terrier, would you give us the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. The Prosecutor is represented by Ms. Sureta Chana, Mr. Michael Blaxill, and Ms. Carmela Annink-Javier and myself, Franck Terrier. Thank you, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Nikola Kostic, and I represent Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General Galic. The Trial Chamber has agreed that I would be designated as the Pre-Trial Judge of this case, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 65 ter, paragraph (A), and in any case my colleagues wanted to sit with me. I know that there are various practices in the different Chambers, but we can always be together and that's all a good thing. Therefore, we are meeting today for the Status Conference in the Galic case, and this Status Conference has several objectives. First of all, it's to review the status of the case; then to organise exchanges between the parties; then to give the possibility to the accused the opportunity to raise any issues relating to his medical condition and his detention conditions. I mention once again detention and health conditions. In order to reach these objectives, I suggest to the parties that we follow the following agenda. These are the large subjects, because after I'm going to take each one of them which has subthemes. The first one would be the status of the case now; then the participation of the Defence in the pre-trial management, that is, Rule 65 ter (F); the calendar, this is an important aspect when we speak about organisation; and then other issues, by that, I mean issues raised by the parties, because as indicated, we must give the floor to General Galic as well. We can begin with the first subject that we have to deal with. The first thing would be to share with the parties the general idea of this Trial Chamber regarding pre-trial management. You know that pre-trial management plays a very important role in the way cases are conducted and the preparation of those cases. We can see, if we look at Rule 65 ter, we reach the conclusion that there are basically two pre-trial phases; the Prosecution's pre-trial phase, which is covered by paragraph (E), and then the pre-trial management for the Defence, which is (J). If you look at the text, you'll see that what is recorded is almost the same. The Prosecution is covered under (E), which is what is required under (G) for the Defence. But there is participation by the Defence in the Prosecutor's pre-trial management; therefore, I'm referring now to paragraph (F). From the point of view of, how can I say this, of general philosophy, of general principles, I think this is what we have to share as a concept so we can work together. From the point of view of objectives, if you look at section (K), under (i) one speaks about a file, and under (ii) there is a second file. By this I mean a file for the Prosecution; another one for the Defence. If you look at paragraph (K), in relation to paragraph (E), as regards the Prosecution, mention is made of a pre-trial brief. This is what I wanted the essential message to be today that I was going to give to you. I was thinking that we should work for the case file, as mentioned under paragraph (K). For the time being, the Prosecutor, and then the Defence, don't have to file a series of briefs in order to begin our work. What I think we can do instead is to work with the parties, discuss the issues that need to be discussed, and most of them are indicated under paragraph (E), and then at the end of the pre-trial phase, set up a case file. I think this would save us a lot of time and save the parties a lot of time, why not say it that way. What I would like to say to the parties is how we're going to work from the point of view of the objectives. What are our working objectives? What are the issues that we've got to discuss between the parties? And what are the conclusions or agreements that we have got to seek? And subsequently, to have all of this in the case file. Therefore, in the pre-trial management -- pre-trial phase of the Prosecution's case, there are subchapters. First would be the disclosure of documents by the Prosecutor; the second would be the preliminary motions; the third point would be consultation between the parties; the fourth would be the list of witnesses for the Prosecution; five, the list of exhibits; six, judicial notice. We're going to go back now to each of these chapters. Disclosure of documents by the Prosecutor, that is, we're referring to the very heart of Rules 66 and 68 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecutor indicated during the Initial Appearance hearing for General Galic that the supporting materials of the indictment would be disclosed on that same day to Defence counsel, in English and in the language of the accused. I would now like to ask the Prosecutor whether this disclosure to the Defence of all of the supporting material has, in fact, been carried out, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 66 of the Rules, and when that was. Mr. Franck Terrier, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The disclosure of the evidence was done completely on the 5th of January of this year, and we received in the following days a receipt from Mr. Kostic. And I believe that these were the commitments taken by the Prosecution before you at the moment of the Initial Appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Terrier. Let me ask the Defence whether it would like to react to what has just been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have received what I believe to be the supporting documents, which I'm led to believe were given to the Judge who authorised the criminal indictment and the warrant at that time. We also have received, subsequent to the date that I received the English version, we also have received a version in the Serbian language, which was given to General Galic for his review. One of the issues that we may have, Your Honour, is the fact that, as I have reviewed the documents that we have received, I did contact Mr. Terrier because I felt that the supporting documents themselves, and I know this is a Status Conference, not an argument, so I'm trying to be somewhat more precise here, that some of the documents were either portions of a longer statement by certain witnesses or attributed to certain witnesses. So parts of them are very short. In other situations, it appeared that the witness had given other statements on the same topic, so we don't know whether that -- what we were given is a summary or a subsequent statement. I contacted Mr. Terrier. He was able to give me a portion of those documents more recently. I don't know the date. But just so you know, I have that. I'm still, however, concerned that there's another aspect of these documents that we feel we should obtain in order to make an intelligent evaluation of whether or not the motions concerning the form of the indictment are appropriate or not. I want to add just one other thing which touches on what we are doing. It doesn't necessarily fall into your agenda, but it's very short, and I'm going to seek the help of the Court. I have continued originally as a temporary assignment Defence counsel, and I still as of today continue as a temporary assignment counsel. That is troublesome to the client because he -- there's an expectation on his part that he would like me to become permanent. He doesn't know what to think of the fact that it's a temporary assignment. And we would seek -- I have not filed a formal motion, Your Honour, but we would like or we would seek some kind of a ruling in regard to the assignment of Defence counsel so that we can proceed. I know that I may be overly technical, and I know that eventually I suspect that the appropriate assignment will be made, but we are now in my third month, and again, as I say, I think for the client's own certainty, it would be good to do that. Again, I apologise for bringing it up a bit outside your agenda, but since we're beginning to meet each other, I thought I would bring it up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, I'm afraid that the Chamber can, perhaps, not help you very much in respect of an appointment of permanent Defence counsel, because this is an issue that falls within the jurisdiction of the Registry. And you should raise that issue either with Ms. Dorothee De Sampayo or Mr. Jean-Jacques Heintz, so that the question can be solved. We can simply say, in support of your concerns, that now we are really working permanently on this case, and as early as possible we've got to settle that question in order for us to be able to work properly. I would ask the registrar to take note of the Trial Chamber's indications so that the Registry is fully aware of our concerns as well. However, there is another question, a series of considerations that perhaps Mr. Terrier is in a position to explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In order to answer Mr. Kostic and to confirm what he just said before the Trial Chamber, I would say that on the 5th of January we disclosed to the Defence 45 statements, which were the statements which the Prosecutor had gathered in support of the indictment. Subsequently, Mr. Kostic asked us for copies of other documents, and we willingly complied with his request, but that disclosure which then came is not covered by Rule 66(A). First of all, that is disclosure which is being carried out kind of beforehand, pursuant to the permanent obligations of Rule 68. So, secondly, we satisfied the disclosure to Mr. Kostic and, of course, we disclosed to them the documents that he asked for. Would you like me to go into more detail in respect of the status of our work for preparing this trial, or would you simply prefer -- well, I had thought about speaking according to the agenda, as you had set it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that would be better. Yes, it would be better. If you allow me, I would prefer it to be that way. Of course, there is some point where you can speak about things that we have not included on the agenda. But for the time being, if you allow, I would prefer to follow the agenda that I set out. I think it would be easier for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, what we can conclude to some extent is that the same materials that the Confirming Judge was able to see in order to confirm the indictment are the same as Mr. Kostic received, and even more; the Prosecutor gave other documents as well. We're clear on that for the time being. Mr. Terrier, I was now going to ask you whether you transmitted to the Defence -- or what measures have been taken in order to transmit copies of witness statements that the Prosecutor has decided to call and the sworn statements, or formal statements, as mentioned in Rule 94 ter. I don't know whether this was something that you wanted to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, it is. It is. That is exactly what I planned to present. In fact, what we did is the following: The Tribunal will remember that the indictment is made up of the following things: First of all, there is a general count which has to do with the campaign of terror which, according to the Prosecution, was carried out against the civilian population of Sarajevo. And in addition, in order to prove that, we put forth a number of specific incidents which occurred during the period covered by the indictment. There are 32 of them as regards the incidents which can be -- which can be ascribable to snipers and six which can relate to shelling. We also have almost completed -- we only have a few -- we have some translation problems in order to complete our work. We constituted a case file for each of those incidents. It's not the Trial Chamber's case file but specific case files for each of the incidents that the Prosecution has to prove during these proceedings at the Tribunal. Each of these case files is made up of statements of eyewitnesses, statements of victims, if they survived, medical certificates, transcripts of investigations when the investigations were carried out, and all other materials which will allow the Judges and the Defence to know where things happened, when things happened, and how things happened. Once all of this has been completed, finalised, we plan to disclose these case files to the Trial Chamber, but at the same time to the Defence as well. And in that way, not only are we setting up and helping in the pre-trial management of the case, but also satisfying our obligations, at least partially our obligations to disclose matters under paragraph 2 of Rule 66. Available to us -- I'm not saying that this is the number of witnesses that we're going to call -- but we've got 180 witnesses, approximately. Eighty-three of the witnesses deal with the incidents that I just mentioned, and they are included in the case files which will be communicate to the Judges and to the Defence. With regards to the others, we are now reviewing which of the witnesses must absolutely be called to the Trial Chamber, in its full bench, and which are the ones that could be invited to submit affidavits according to the procedures which will be defined by the Trial Chamber, and who are the ones who, if necessary, could be heard on the basis of Rule 71 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Therefore, we are now doing this work, and as soon as it is done, we will, of course, be able to inform the Trial Chamber thereof. It is very important for us, for the Trial Chamber, and for the subsequent Status Conferences, that once each of the incidents that been transmitted in the case file, after having the time to review them carefully, we have to be told which are the ones that are considered as being proved and which are being contested, and, in the end, what the Prosecutor is going to have to prove according to the forms provided for in the Rules of Procedure. Therefore, we are at that stage, and of course in order for this pre-trial management to be conducted as quickly and effectively as important, it's very important for us and for the Trial Chamber and for the Defence that the Defence team be set up as quickly as possible. We cannot remain as we are now, where Mr. Kostic has his contract renewed from month to month without being certain of his future, and this is not a situation which is proper for the accused himself. Therefore, this is where we are, and I hope in that way the Prosecutor will make an effective contribution to the pre-trial management and in accordance with the desires expressed by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Terrier. You have spoken about the Defence team, which is a good thing, because we have to think not only about Mr. Kostic but also about the co-counsel, and I think that the Registry will take care of that issue, because it is true that we really must work on this case. And this is what the Trial Chamber believes and, more specifically, what the Pre-Trial Judge believes. Mr. Terrier, if I understood you correctly, in respect of the components of Rule 66(i)(a), will two weeks, 15 days, be enough in order to complete that work?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifteen days -- well, what we don't have yet for these case files are the translations. That's never an easy problem in this Tribunal, as Your Honours know. But we also need to supplement them with maps. What we want is that the Judges, the Defence, and the Prosecution, when they open the case file, know exactly what happened during that incident. And for this reason -- what we don't have are those maps. Everything else has been put together. I would also like to say that in certain cases, if possible -- it won't always be possible, of course, because places have changed -- but we would like there to be photographs or photographic reports of the situation, of the locations. Fifteen days is a little short to me. Your Honour, if possible, I would be obliged to have four weeks. Four weeks would be more to my liking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could give you three weeks and with a week's grace period. That would be a specific objective, three weeks, and then we would permit, if you are not in a position to do otherwise, one extra week. Would that be all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll try to do the best we can to do it in three weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I now set that time limit with the manoeuvrability.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour. There is still the translation problem. We don't completely control that. You know that there's moving that's now going on, and things are becoming a bit more complicated and will be complicated in the coming days and weeks. Perhaps we'll need that grace period for the translation. But other than that, it should be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in any case, since we are now speaking about time limits and we have a chapter devoted to the calendar, perhaps we could go back to that at the proper moment, if you agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Terrier. Let me now turn to the Defence. Mr. Kostic, I don't know if you are in a position to answer a question that we have. Are you going to file a request to consult those materials covered under 66(B), and if so, well, then, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in regard to a request under Rule 66(B), I would expect that we may be able to file a request very quickly. In fact, I would like to do that even within the two weeks' time period. In addition, you should know, as long as we're -- well, I'll keep it at that. I think that we'll do that within the two weeks' period, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could continue, Mr. Kostic. If you think that you're going to file a request or motion, perhaps it would be better to consult with the Prosecutor, with Mr. Terrier, about that. I think that as a general rule, we're going to adopt that procedure. Whenever there is a brief, the parties have to consult in order to know whether or not they can reach an agreement. If they do and if the Trial Chamber recognises it, then it will. But if there is an agreement that the Trial Chamber doesn't have to know about, then we won't have a problem either. So I think it would be better for Mr. Kostic to consult the Prosecutor, and in any case, so that things be clear, I'm going to ask Mr. Franck Terrier whether he agrees to that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Mr. President. I think that's the spirit of Rule 66(B). Mr. Kostic merely has to send us a letter, and we'll make ourselves available to him and make available to him anything that we have, all documents, books, photographs, et cetera, subject, of course, to reciprocity provided by the Rules. I wanted to clarify something. I was wondering whether there might be something confused here having to do with preliminary motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nothing to do with preliminary motions. No more confusion here. Mr. Kostic, that is your answer. You can consult with the Prosecutor about that possibility, that you might want to use Rule 66(B), because this is a request of the Defence. Therefore, you seem to be going down the same road as Mr. Terrier. We'll work on that together. I was going to now move to point 2; that is, the preliminary motions. Pursuant to 72(A), as you know, Mr. Kostic, the 30-day time period for filing preliminary motions runs from the date that the exhibits -- the supporting material for the indictment was communicated, and as you know, the date mentioned here is the 5th of January. Thirty days, the 5th of February, no preliminary motions have been filed to date. Does the Defence confirm that it has not filed preliminary motions, and does it have any comments to make on that subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in regard to the preliminary motions, there were two concerns; one I've already talked about, which is the issue of my own appointment, which you're familiar with, and I won't go beyond that. As far as the other preliminary motions that need to be raised, those will be filed perhaps as early as this afternoon or tomorrow. My only issue does go back, and I think that that has to do with the issue that we talked about, which is whether there's a feeling by the Defence that we have been provided everything that we need to have to argue the motion as to the jurisdictional issue, which is the form of the indictment, without the documents which I have talked about. I will file a motion as to that jurisdictional issue. The problem, of course, is that I have to, in arguing that motion without the documentation, which I think I may or I may not get in the next -- I think we're at two weeks, the last time I heard. Those witness statements, I think, are important. What I would like to do, with the exception -- the other motions will be filed today or tomorrow. As far as the jurisdictional motion is concerned, I'm going to be filing it, preserving our right to add to it, and what I would like to do is to have some additional time to do that once I receive the materials from Mr. Terrier, because I think that it again -- it's hard to respond. The only thing I can do, Your Honour, and I can do that within two weeks, is I can file -- in addition to the jurisdictional motion, arguing what I'm saying, and that is the inability to argue the sufficiency of the indictment without the additional documents, whether it's because of the statements or out of context, but I can make that argument. I hope I'm clear. If I'm not clear, I will certainly be here to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is that the time period has already lapsed. There is no time period, Mr. Kostic. The time period lapsed on the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The only thing I can do is to file -- most of the motions -- I can file a motion to extend and see if the Chamber rules on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you do your work. The Pre-Trial Judge or the Trial Chamber needn't tell you what you're supposed to do. But if you look at the Tribunal's case law carefully in respect of preliminary motions, I think that you will reach the conclusion that you have other work to do. I don't know if you're going to file a preliminary motion in order to call into question the Tribunal's jurisdiction or the defects in the form of the indictment. Perhaps I could invite you to review the Tribunal's case law, and perhaps I could give you another possibility. There might be other work to do. In any case, if you file a motion, the Judges will have to rule on it; that is true. But it is also true that the time period for filing the preliminary motions has already elapsed, and it elapsed on the 5th of February. I ask you to reflect on this. I don't want this to constitute pressure or any kind of direction that the Defence has to take. The Defence has to take its own decisions. But I want you to be fully aware of what the situation is. We're going to move now -- well, I don't want to end that issue without giving the floor back to Mr. Terrier. What is the position of the Prosecutor in respect of this issue of the time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor must only refer to the rules of procedure that you've mentioned, specifically the provisions of Rule 72. If Mr. Kostic wanted an extension of the time period, then he should have asked it of the Trial Chamber within the proper time period. He can't ask for an extension once that period for doing so has been elapsed for a long time. I have no further comments to make at this time, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, we're now going to move to the third subject of the Pre-Trial Status Conference for the Prosecution, pre-trial phase of the Prosecution. That is the issue of consultation between the parties. I think this is becoming part of our culture here at the Tribunal, that is, the Trial Chambers and specifically this Trial Chamber, to ask for good cooperation between the parties, and I'm saying this to you because the Chamber believes that the role of the Defence is not a passive one, that is, one where it puts itself into a position of waiting for what the Prosecution is going to do. But the Prosecutor must prove his accusations, and the Defence puts itself into a passive attitude of waiting. I think that we must really have a different vision of the situation. By that I mean that the Defence must defend, and I say this so that we can have proper justice. We've got proper justice when somebody who makes an accusation does that with somebody defending as well. The Defence has an active role to play, an active defence in its position. One doesn't ordinarily use this kind of language in a courtroom, but I would say that ordinarily in football, teams that are -- defensive teams and those who only defend usually lose the match. I think we've got to have this idea of active defence in mind. That means that there must be discussions between the parties, the parties have to talk about the issues together. So we have now reached, if I could say it this way, the objectives of the pre-trial management. We have to know -- and Mr. Terrier has already touched on that issue -- we must know what are the points of dispute and what are the points of agreement. What are the points of fact and law in respect of litigious questions and those for which there is an agreement. Why do I say or ask that? Because if we know which points are in disagreement, what are the points being disputed in respect of fact and law, we'll have defined the purpose of the trial. That is what I want the parties to understand. That is, that there must be exchanges, there must be discussions, you must work together. Why do I say this? Well, at least so that we can know where we stand in respect of agreements and where we stand in respect of disagreements. And there may be something else as well. It may be that I don't agree with this account of something on the whole but partially in agreement; that is, I would agree that something happened and I agree that these events happened, but I do not agree, for instance, that my client was there or was not at that place but rather in another place. All of that can be the subject of discussions. Therefore, we must start with that provision. Let me give you another idea, the point of view of cooperation between the parties. There is only cooperation when there is the availability to be cooperative. If I want to cooperate but the other party doesn't want to, then it's ridiculous to continue cooperating with somebody who doesn't want to cooperate, and I'll defend myself as well. But if I want to cooperate and the other party does as well, well, that much the better, because that's what we wanted from the very outset. This has to do with what was enshrined as being the win/win strategy, because at the end both parties cooperating with one another both win. Another idea that I would like to indicate, from a practical point of view -- what I'm saying here are points of reference. But you are familiar with the case, you are familiar with the situation. You can find other ways of working. But let me give you this way of looking at things: To begin with, perhaps we should read together the indictment and say, "Yes, I agree with those." "No, I don't agree with that." "No, I don't agree, or here perhaps I could admit to this part, but the other part I can't accept." This is a practical way of reaching agreements and understanding which are the disagreements. Another idea in this chapter or subchapter having to do with consulting between the parties, the Trial Chamber considers this procedure: Any motion that a party wants to file must be discussed first with the other party. If there's an agreement, fine, then there's an agreement. If it's necessary that the Trial Chamber render a decision, then you'll tell us. You tell us, "I ask this. I spoke with the other party, and there's an agreement." And then the Trial Chamber would verify whether the agreement complies with the Rules and principles or whether, to the contrary, if one were to say, "I've discussed these things, but the other party does not agree, and so I put this to the finding of the Trial Chamber." And then the Trial Chamber will essentially and always, as far as possible, render oral decisions. This is a tradition that I took from another case, that all motions were filed orally and the decisions were rendered orally. This goes more quickly for everybody. Lastly, let me remind you that the written conclusions on the points of agreement and disagreement relating to questions of fact and law must be drafted in accordance with the provisions of Rule 65 ter (H). But we'll get to that later. I would now like to have reactions in order to close this subchapter relating to consultations between the parties. I'd like to have the parties' reactions now. Mr. Franck Terrier, would you like to say something to us? Do you agree with us or do you not agree with us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely agree, Mr. President, with the general guidelines that you have sketched out, and I think that this corresponds to what we feel. I think with regard to all these points, what you have said is very useful and enables the Defence to be completely informed, broadly informed, on what the Prosecution is doing and the evidence that it relies on. And we're going to communicate not only witness statements, which we are bound to do through the Rules, but also other documents as well, especially such as plans, medical reports, and other documents of that type. Once the Defence has been fully and completely informed, I think that it will be able to take an active part, and the Defence will be able to tell us what it agrees with and accepts and if there is anything it wishes to contest. But I would like to assure the Chamber that these relations will follow those guidelines, and I hope that we will have as broad an agreement as possible. Of course, it can never be absolutely complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Terrier. I should like to thank you for those proposals. Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I wish I could discuss with you the philosophy about football, but maybe for some other time. I think that I would be available to consult and try to reach agreements in this case. What I think you probably appreciate my situation at this time is I know really very little about the case itself on the basis of the fact that I only have the supporting documents which were given to me, as you know. I do not know -- in fact, today is the first day that I heard the number of 180 witnesses that are potential witnesses in this case. From the indictment I have a general idea, perhaps, or I can attempt to analyse the theory of the Prosecution as to why my client may be potentially guilty -- charged and guilty of any or all of these counts. But I'm really a little bit behind the Prosecutor, probably some five or six years behind him, in regard to this particular case, but the way I like to practice law is to stay in contact with the Prosecutor, meet with him, attempt to reach agreements if we can, obviously consulting with Mr. Galic, because as you can imagine, he's an integral part in any of those discussions. And I think we can, where possible, reach agreements. Where we can't, obviously we'll have to do the best we can to present arguments to you, and you'll have to rule. So I think it's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kostic. Let us now move on to the fourth chapter of the witness list of the Prosecutor. As we know, Article 65 ter, and in view of the philosophy of the Rules and not football now, we have Rule 65 ter (i). So we have all this about the pre-trial management. And if we look at (iv), a list of witnesses stating the names and pseudonyms of each witness. It is (a). I don't know whether I'm going to go through all this and whether I'm going to take it point by point or look at it in its entirety and have your reactions after that, perhaps. But if we look at (a), the name or pseudonym of each witness in that particular Rule, and I think it would be useful if the Prosecutor would furnish a list of witnesses who would like protective measures and to tell us what kind of protective measures he would like to have. I think this would be very useful with regard to the entire proceedings because this would enable us to know in advance who the witness is, what protection he or she is requiring and bring this to the attention of the public and say a day in advance that there will be a public hearing or not, because we have to respect our public, of course, the public attending the proceedings and the trial. So if we have the name or pseudonym of each witness, a complete list, and if protective measures are required, if you could say so in advance, straight away. So if there is an agreement reached on this point beforehand, together with the Defence counsel, then these protective measures will be accorded and then we shall be able to state for each witness what protective measures have been undertaken, whether they are using a name or pseudonym, and all this can be regulated before the actual start of the trial itself. Perhaps I should refer to some of the other points in the Rule, and (b) is a summary on the facts on which each witness will testify. If the Prosecutor is going to make a summary, I would like to draw the Prosecution's attention to the following: In my experience so far of the summaries that we have had to date, we did indeed receive summaries, but they had very little to do with (c), that is to say, the points in the indictment as to which each witness will testify, including specific references to counts and relevant paragraphs in the indictment. I know that this is not always the case, of course, but I do feel that those summaries must be compiled by the team presenting them, because if the Prosecutor says to an investigator, "Give me a summary," he is going to make a summary of the statements, but perhaps that particular individual will not be aware of the important points. Therefore, I consider that a summary of facts really means what it says: a summary of important facts, facts which are important vis-à-vis the indictment. Therefore, I think we ought to understand points (b) and (c) of Rule 65 ter in an coordinated fashion. Then we come to (d), which is the estimated length of time required for each witness. I know that it is very difficult to calculate in advance, because there are many things that are outside our control. But if we are able to estimate the length of time, that would be a good time. Having said that, I would like to go back to a another little question, a point, which I think Mr. Terrier mentioned a moment ago when he spoke about Article 71 and the presiding officer, and I think this had to do with the classification itself. I'm sure that you will not be leading the Trial Chamber astray. I think that all the points were important. So what is the question actually?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fourmy is drawing my attention to the fact that there was no transcript in English. Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: Something is wrong with my cord. Everything is recorded, but it's not spitting through yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, is what we're saying being recorded, however?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have Mr. Kostic here, who is listening to the proceedings in English. Are things all right now?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. What I was saying, I was speaking about what we could talk about classifying witnesses, classification of witnesses. As you know, the Trial Chamber can take a decision to shorten the list of witnesses. I think the Trial Chamber should not choose the Prosecution's or the Defence's witness, but, rather, it's the party's responsibility to get the information to the Chambers so that they can shorten the list, if necessary. I think this classification -- I know that Mr. Terrier is familiar with that, that is, classifying witnesses as important, more less important, and less important, and then to choose those witnesses which are less important and perhaps some who are more or less important in order to hear their testimony through a presiding officer. Now we're only speaking about the general outlines of the trial, and what I'm expecting from the Prosecutor in this case -- don't answer me that all witnesses are important, please, I do believe that -- but the question is to know which witnesses are the ones who are going to come to testify and which are the ones who are going to testify through a presiding officer, because they also will continue to be important. It's from that point of view of organisation that I'm speaking, and I'm not going to go into that question in any further detail. The expert witnesses. Well, all right, I think that either the Prosecution or the Defence is familiar with 94 bis, and so I don't have to ask the Prosecutor whether there is a great deal to report. But it's simply to point out that this question has been raised. And before we move to the fifth subchapter, I would like to give the parties an opportunity to react to the list of the Prosecutor. Do you agree or do you not agree? Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor will try not to disappoint the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position is the following: We have 180 witnesses who have been identified as being able to provide useful information to the Judges in this case. Naturally, all of these witnesses are important, but not all of them have to provide the information according to the same procedure, the same ways. I was speaking about case files dealing with specific incidents, either of snipers or shelling. We have about 80 witnesses who have to do with those incidents. If it should happen that the Defence agrees that these incidents did, in fact, take place, according to the circumstances as presented by the Prosecutor, it does not intend to contest that on such and such a date, a shelling against the civilian population happened and that this number of people died at this place or at that time, while they were waiting in line to get some water or they were at the market. If of those incidents or if some of them are not being challenged, then of course that witness will not be heard before this Trial Chamber, that is, heard by three Judges. But, of course, these are still important witnesses. In addition, and this is perhaps a specific characteristic of this case, it is possible that we can define categories of witnesses as being very specific, very differentiated. We've got those witnesses who were members of UNPROFOR, others who were civilian officials, and others who were military officials. There were journalists. There were dignitaries representing the communities of Sarajevo. We can differentiate things very easily in respect of those different categories of witnesses and say that we make proposals in this way; that is, to say that some of the categories or some of the representatives of these different witness categories have to be heard by all three Judges; others can provide affidavits; and still others, if the Trial Chamber agrees, can be heard through a Presiding Officer. This, in my opinion, is a procedure which would be perfectly acceptable to the Defence insofar as the Defence is exercising all its rights. I know about the discussion on affidavits. I know Mr. Kostic may object to the affidavit, and I do understand that very easily. However, as regards proceedings covered by 71, Mr. Kostic will be there in order to cross-examine the witness, and, therefore, the rights of the accused will be fully respected. We are working in that way, and I hope that it will satisfy the Chamber. We will make proposals as to the list of witnesses of those that have to be heard by all of the Judges and those that can be heard through the 71 provisions. But before we get to that point, I think it would be a good thing for the Defence to tell us what it agrees to and what it does not agree to so that we will know what direction to take. Of course, it goes without saying that many of the facts and circumstances mentioned by the Prosecution, if they are challenged, then the trial, of course, will be one in which more witnesses are going to have to come, and that's just how things go. That's just the rules of the game. That should not constitute pressure on the Defence. In any case, that's how we are working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Terrier. Mr. Kostic, would you like to make any comments, or do you have any reactions to what has just been said in respect of the list of the Prosecutor's witnesses, and specifically to what Mr. Terrier has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it might be too early for me to have an opinion in regard to the statement by the Prosecutor, because, as you know, as I said before, I know very little about the case now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We understand very well, Mr. Kostic, but we do consider you a party to your discussions, of course, and that is precisely why I always ask for your opinions, and I am very pleased to have you. We can now move forward to the fifth subchapter, if you like, and that is the list of exhibits, that is to say, 65 ter (E)(i) or -- no, it is (v) and it is what exhibits the Prosecutor intends to offer. What I would like to say is that regard is we have tried in another case, we have tried to do something with some results. And in order to distribute our time well, once again to prepare in advance the list of exhibits. So that when we come to the courtroom, the registrar should already know the numbers, the exhibits have already been marked, so that when the Prosecutor develops his arguments and brings up an exhibit, he places it on the ELMO and everybody will know which exhibit it is because it will have a number. I think that this is something that we tried to do. I don't know what the practice has been of other Trial Chambers, but we have used it in our own Trial Chamber, and I think that we had a great deal of success with that and were able to save time. Because if every time the Prosecutor presents an exhibit he has to open a file, takes out a piece of paper, asks the registrar to present it to the Defence counsel, to the Judge and so on, and if we multiply this time by the number of exhibits, we get an exorbitant figure and loss of time. So I think it will be possible with the registrar, who has this experience already, to go ahead with this kind of practice. I should like the two parties, the Defence and the Prosecution, to organise the exhibits so that they are ready for the trial and the testimony and can be used straight away. So I think that was the guiding light or idea that I wanted to state with respect to this question, but I'd like to hear your reactions. Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are aware of the advantages of this practice, and of course we will comply with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Kostic, you'll see how that is going to work, and you'll conclude that things work well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I agree with what you have just said. Your colleague on the Bench, Judge Wald, know how the practice is in the Federal Courts of the United States, and what you have just said is exactly the way they do it, so I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are very pleased to hear that, because we were convinced that we had discovered something and it functioned very well. So we are going to use this procedure as well. This brings me to another question, and perhaps there will be a lot of space to discuss this opinion. Judicial notice. If we look at Article 94, referring to judicial notice, and it is divided into two parts, we have facts of common knowledge, proof of facts of common knowledge on the one part, and we also have adjudicated facts or documentary evidence from other proceedings of the Tribunal relating to matters at issue in the current proceedings. I don't think I can go further than that at present because the parties will undertake exchanges, of course, and will find either something to say with regard to (A) or with regard to (B) of Article 94, and we'll see possibilities in both, and indeed in going further afield as well. And I think that if we speak of jurisprudence, we can also look at the practice that was relevant to another case, where judicial notice was brought up and where 583 pieces of fact came to light, and the Chamber agreed on judicial notice on 470 facts -- pieces of evidence. I don't need to tell you that this requires a great deal of time, a great deal of money, and a great deal of witnesses and witness testimony. So for the moment I wanted to give this to the parties to consider, to look into all the possibilities of utilising this judicial notice that stands at their disposal: either proof of facts of common knowledge or judicial notice of adjudicated facts or documentary evidence from other proceedings. I do not know whether you wish to react in this regard. Perhaps, Mr. Terrier, you would like to at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My first reaction, since we're still not really quite sure about what our position on judicial notice is, which is a difficult one even theoretically, and about which people might have different and conflicting opinions. First of all, if we are, during our discussions with the Defence, able to agree to a certain number of facts, I think it would be very easy for the Judges to take note of this, whether it be in the form of a judicial notice, under Rule 94, or in another form. It would, I hope, be a matter of facts that took place within Sarajevo as part of that period covered by the indictment. There is another issue, which we think that we must submit to this Trial Chamber's Judges, and that is that some of the evidence was gathered by another group in this Tribunal, although some of the Judges here were part of that bench of Judges. As part of the 61 proceedings, which were carried out on the basis of the indictment against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, during those 61 proceedings, which was not an inter partes proceedings, the parties agreed that what was in question was Sarajevo itself. And we wanted to make sure that this evidence can be submitted as part of these proceedings without necessarily having to have those witnesses to be called back. I think that would be useful and I think that the rights of the Defence would be preserved insofar as Mr. Kostic or another Defence representative could discuss with both parties present about that evidence. If Mr. Kostic wanted a witness to be called back, of course the Trial Chamber would decide whether it is appropriate or necessary. But in any case, the rights of the Defence would be respected by open discussion before the Judges in respect of the validity, relevance, and scope of that evidence. But I think about individuals, I'm thinking about a representative of the civilian community in Sarajevo, who spoke in one of these 61 proceedings about the fact that there really was a siege, that during that siege, he could speak about what the population had experienced. And all of this goes back to Count 1 of the indictment, that is, the complain of terror against a civilian population. There is that testimony, but there is other testimony as well, and I'm essentially thinking about those proceedings. Perhaps there are other procedures and proceedings that can be used during which useful and appropriate evidence was gathered. But I can't say anything further about that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, do you have any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think on a number of the issues in regard to judicial notice I would like to reserve some later opinion because I'm not sure what all will come into play. But my understanding of the Rule 61 hearing here some time ago is a little bit like a football match but only one team played. It was not a full match. And I think that would, of course, bother me if anything of a judicial notice nature would be then awarded as a category from that. However -- however, I will certainly meet with the Prosecutor, and if there is something within any of those documents and/or statements that we could potentially agree on, I would be prepared to do that. I just had a reaction because of the nature of that hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would simply like to take advantage of this time to tell you that in another case that the Trial Chamber is hearing, the parties agreed that they would tender some of the excerpts from the 61 hearing, that is, the Karadzic and Mladic hearings. I'm only giving you that information now. Before we leave -- well, in order to talk about the second chapter of the Defence's participation in pre-trial management and in respect of exhibits, I know that this is a very open question and one which is difficult to talk about. But the question I would like to raise is the following: Among the documents and the testimony, ordinarily we're able to establish some kind of a relationship that a document has been presented and is valid if it has been presented through a witness. I don't know whether the parties want to think about this possibility; that is, the documents will be worth what they're worth; the testimony will be worth what it's worth. And if there are no questions about authenticity in respect of the document, why present it always through a witness? I throw that question out to you so that you can think about it, because frequently we waste time reading the documents when all of us know exactly how to read, and the witness is reading for us. We know how to read. But I know that this is a question which may not be absolutely or equally shared from people coming from two different legal systems, that is, the common law and the civil law systems. As you know, we have done away with them a long time ago, in fact, the discussion about common and civil law. We have our own Rules, we have our own case law, and in the light of this and in the light of the Tribunal's objectives and the principles of law, couldn't we think about that? I throw that question out to you for your reflection. And now I move to the second chapter, that is, the Defence participation in pre-trial management, that is, Rule 65 ter (F). Perhaps Mr. Kostic is not in a position to answer today, but as I said to you at the outset, we would like to share with the parties some ideas which could then be used. Here is a question: Does the Defence plan to put forth any alibi defence, pursuant to Rule 67? I'll, first of all, ask all questions, and then Mr. Kostic can tell us whether he is in a position to answer today. The other question, outside from the defence of alibi, is Rule 65 ter, under paragraph (F); that is, "(i) in general terms, the nature of the accused's defence." At the end of the pre-trial stage, the Defence must be prepared to tell us, in general terms, what the nature of the accused's defence is. The matters with which the accused takes issue in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief, and for each of these points the reason why the accused takes issue, that is, there are conclusions which can be reached after the exchanges. There is another point that I would like to ask you to think about, that is, ask the Defence to think about, that is, the accused testifying; yes or no, and if yes, when? That is, we have already -- we already have a practice here in this Tribunal, according to which the accused who have decided to testify in their own defence did so after the preliminary statements of the Prosecution. I can tell you that I have had the experience of General Blaskic's case, and I was absolutely struck by the fact that we heard almost three months of testimony by General Blaskic, only to learn that he was not challenging what the Prosecutor had tried to prove over a great period of time, with a great many exhibits and many witnesses; that is, there can be some advantage, even for the accused, to testify in his own defence at the beginning of the trial, but it is something which Mr. Galic's Defence will have to decide. I would like to tell you that the Trial Chamber will not bring any pressure to bear in that respect, but we just wish to state the experience we have had and which tells us that it is a good solution and that we have already practised it. We have had experience of the accused testifying immediately after the opening statements by the Prosecution. Well, there we have, Mr. Kostic, a series of questions and guidelines for the Defence. I don't know whether you wish to react now or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Of course I should react because it is a Status Conference and it would be good to give you my own thoughts about that, and partially they are also based on some sort of natural instincts after many years of practising criminal defence law. So I'm sort of apologising ahead of time for those natural reactions. As far as an alibi defence is concerned, of course I do need to see all of the documents and the accusations, and if, in fact, there is testimony, statements of witnesses, which place Mr. Galic at a certain location that he disputes. Generally, I can tell you that to interpose an alibi defence for some two and a half years of alleged activity is difficult for me to perceive doing, but there may be some potential for some shorter period of time. That's based, again, on looking at the discoveries, I call them discovery materials. The other question that you've asked me is probably a bit more interesting, and I know that you've made some interesting comments about the common law and the civil law, criminal procedure, whether or not defendants or the accused testify in their own trials. You know that I come from a system which has certain guarantees and the right to remain silent, and all of that. We generally, again, do like to see all of the discovery materials before we discuss with a client whether or not he wants to testify. There are some issues also in regard to the Statute and the Rules and regulations in the present system, something called the presumption of innocence and the right to remain silent. So I have to analyse that in light of what you have just said, and if there is a practice here that I feel I have to follow, and which is, of course, the Court's practice. As such, I have to adapt or modify my natural reactions. So having said that, I can still tell you this: That I find, again, from some theoretical and practice pointers, that I certainly would not like to have a client testify before all of the Prosecution case is finished, and then I have to make a decision whether he is the first or the last witness. There are pluses in that regard in both ways. I will keep in mind your comments and certainly tell you well ahead of time. I also think, Judge or Judges, as I deal with the Prosecutor in identifying the points of agreement and the points of dispute, obviously if my client's going to testify, he would be aware of all of those facts, and therefore I wouldn't want to have a client testify for three days or three months who is going to say that he agrees with some aspects of what the Prosecutor has already introduced. So keeping that in mind, I think that we can do that. I think that in this kind of a Tribunal, with the issues that we're dealing with, with the accusations that we're dealing with, I would imagine that -- I shouldn't say "imagine"; that's a bad word. I would predict that a client would probably testify, or most likely. I'm trying to be as complete and as clear with you this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kostic. As I gave the floor to Mr. Kostic for accusation matters, I now give the floor to Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just have one comment to make about what Mr. Kostic said and what you said. I do understand Mr. Kostic's position today, in light of the fact that he does not yet know what exhibits and evidence the Prosecution has. I would say that if it were to be that the accused and Defence counsel's position were to be that General Galic were to testify at the start of the trial, after the opening statements, I think that the possibility should be reserved to the Prosecution to cross-examine after the testimony has been finished, because I don't think it would be good to cross-examine right at the beginning, before other evidence had been presented to the full Chamber of Judges. That's my only concern. If Mr. Kostic wants his client to testify or not, that's his right, and the Prosecution will simply take note of that. But if the Defence wants Mr. Galic to testify at the beginning or the end, I think the Prosecution has no preferences to make. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Terrier. I specifically would like to thank you for having recalled to me that in practice, it is true that the accused testified at the start of the trial but that the Prosecutor has the cross-examination after other evidence has been presented, and that's as you have just said and I thank you very much for that, Mr. Terrier. I myself, at this point, have a question, because I see that we have now been working for an hour and a half, and my question is: Shall we take a break and then come back and continue work a little bit, for another 15 minutes, or should be go directly to the end and we would only have to work for another 15 minutes or so. Yes, we can continue. We're all working together, solidarity, you see, because we've all worked all day long. We're all tired, and that's why I thank everybody. All right. Let's now move to a more interesting chapter, that is, the calendar. The purpose of the calendar that I'm going to propose to you is to determine the -- to set the pre-trial management as quickly as possible, according to the matters that we've discussed with you today, giving the parties the time needed in order to prepare themselves, so that we can set the temporal conditions for discussing the various issues and the time it's going to take for people to meet. In order to reach those objectives -- that is, the calendar is a bit tight because we want to finish as quickly as we can. Several dates have as their purpose giving to the parties, even physically speaking, time that they can meet in order to discuss things, so we have to have dates and locations, because it isn't possible to reach an agreement or to not reach an agreement if people can't discuss things with one another. In order to do so, there must be time and there must be a location to do so. Therefore, in respect of the calendar, the first point, we will consider a working period of about one month and a half for each of the parties to study everything that's been discussed and all the directions that have been given. Each of the parties can work, and among other things, the parties can exchange information with one another. If we consider one and a half months, there are then four dates for Status Conferences: The 30th of May, the 1st of June, the 5th of June, and the 8th of June. The purpose of this is to see where we stand and possibly to start discussions going again between the parties and to find the points for which there is agreement and for which there is not agreement; that is, you have a month and a half in order to work on all of those questions, even exchanging information. And then you would have two weeks at the Tribunal and you would come to the first Status Conference and say, "We're here. We've reached this agreement" or "We haven't reached this agreement," and then we could discuss matters and perhaps we would find other alternatives. The parties would work, come back with results, then we would review those results, and then we could go back to certain questions that have not been resolved. That's what I mean when I say that we need time and space to discuss matters. The work would be done between the parties and the Pre-Trial Judge. The third point regarding the calendar is the 10th of July, that particular date, for filing any motions of the Prosecution, preliminary motions or anything of that kind, by the Prosecution. On the 24th of July, that would be the date on filing the preliminary motions with respect to the Defence, Defence preliminary motions. The 1st of September would be the date for a Pre-Trial Conference; that is to say, the Pre-Trial Conference, because we might need other days as well. In order to conclude -- the 1st of September is a fixed date. The Pre-Trial Judge would like to have concluded, by that date, all the preliminary proceedings, and of course the other dates can be modified. I'm telling you this now because I have sketched out this calendar with one particular objective, and that is that we should finish our work by the 1st of September. I have formed the habit of working in that way. We must have an objective for our work. So let's put that deadline as the 1st of September. Once we have that date, we can look at the proceedings that have taken place, and that is the date by which we should have finished all our work. So this is our objective, the 1st of September. That is our target. What is important for us at the moment is to say that this particular date, the 1st of September, is the date by which we should have concluded all the preliminary proceedings and stand trial-ready. If the Chamber -- whether the Trial Chamber can go ahead or not, that's another question. But I would like to have all preliminary matters decided by the 1st of September. That is the deadline. May I have your reactions now, please. Mr. Terrier, what do you have to say to that calendar and those dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a question I would like to ask. Of course I do I understand the Trial Chamber today cannot set a date for the beginning of the trial, but could you give us an approximate period? About how much time could elapse once pre-trial matters have been completed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I can say -- well, I don't know if I can say it in public -- what I can say is that we are trying to find a solution possibly to resolve matters in respect of what we call a queuing system, that there would be trials that are ready, having the availability of the Trial Chamber to start that trial. My strategy now, that is, the Chamber's strategy, is to have the case trial-ready. If the Chamber is going to take it, that's another issue. But if we are going to take up the case, I must tell you that it cannot begin before January of 2001, and that's being very optimistic. As you know, the Chamber is simultaneously hearing two cases, and it may be that, for exceptional reasons, one case must be stopped -- one never knows -- and then we could begin with Galic if the case is trial-ready. Those are the two reasons why we need to have this case trial-ready, because the Trial Chamber might have the possibility of starting the case or another Chamber might be in a position to do so. These are the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have another question to ask, which is connected with the calendar. As I was saying, we are going to define which of the witnesses we believe could help justice through 61 hearings. It is not indicated under 61 -- or 71, excuse me. It could be during the parallel judgements or it could also be during the pre-trial phase, under Rule 71. But in any case, nothing is contraindicative that in Rule 71 -- but I was wondering whether this trial, with the full bench of Judges, if it were to begin, wouldn't it be possible that the Chamber could decide, without waiting for that date, that time period, and that as part of pre-trial management, witnesses could be heard by one of the Trial Chamber's Judges or a Presiding Officer before that time, as part of the pre-trial phase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that's a possibility that we could consider, although I myself -- I'm speaking for myself now -- I would prefer to have the trial begin, and then at the period where the Prosecution makes its case, to have those witnesses called in to testify before Presiding Officers, and the same thing would be for the Defence. Once the exculpatory evidence has been presented, at the same time we could have depositions through a Presiding Officer. But I think that can be discussed, and even the parties could provide some thoughts about that. I don't know what my colleagues' feelings are about that, but we are open to that possibility. That's what I can say now. Thank you. Mr. Kostic, does this calendar suit you? We know that you have many commitments and I know that at least on two occasions we had to postpone Status Conferences. We would very much like you to have the chance to plan things, to programme your schedule, because schedules are important so that people know what they have to do. It's not a programme for the Defence or for Mr. Kostic, but rather one which helps us all to do our work properly. Do you have any comments to make, or any objections you would like to raise, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: As far as the date that you have mentioned, which is June 8th as another Status Conference, that is a date that is something that is within my calendar; it's open. So that's a date that's a good date. As far as the case in general, in terms of your expectations, it's very hard for me to give you an opinion. As far as the September 1 date, I suppose some of it depends on how extensive the discovery materials are and the witnesses, the number of witness statements that we would get, and so on. If you're asking me for an opinion -- and Judges usually don't, you know, in regard to scheduling and so on; they have their own work and their own cases to handle -- I would suggest that we would need an extra 30 days, looking at this particular case, just from what we've talked about today and what I know about it so far, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to take advantage of what Mr. Kostic has just said. This is a Chamber which exercises its authority but not in an authoritarian manner. We always ask for the opinion of the parties. Likewise, in the way that I answered Mr. Terrier, I would like to say that the calendar is an instrument, is a working tool, and we are available -- I'm speaking for myself as the Pre-Trial Judge -- available to review the calendar if it's necessary. I do prefer to stick to that calendar, that is, the 1st of September. And once Mr. Kostic is in a position to conclude that he really needs additional time -- because I believe, Mr. Kostic, that perhaps you're going to need time after the presentation of exculpatory evidence by the Prosecutor -- if Mr. Kostic or if Mr. Franck Terrier meet and agree that this calendar is not good and has to be changed, then we will. The parties merely have to indicate this to the Pre-Trial Judge. All right. We'll stay with that programme, which has objectives for our work. But it's a working instrument. We are not slaves to a programme; the programme should be used to serve us. If it doesn't, then we've got to change it, it's got to be discussed. But I think for the time being we've got to have a working plan, and this is what I want to leave in the parties' hands. Let me move now to the final chapter so that we can really end our work. The interpreters are still alive, I hope. Yes. And now it's the issue of other questions. Are there any other questions to be raised by the parties, questions which we have not dealt with under the points already discussed? Or is that all for the time being?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very briefly. Within the time period that you said at the beginning of this hearing, we will disclose to the Defence, and of course to the Trial Chamber, the case files which were constituted for each of the incidents mentioned in the indictment. What we are requesting from the Trial Chamber as an order -- but we intend to speak about this with Mr. Kostic once this hearing is over; we're going to have a discussion with him -- is, in a very traditional way, to order protective measures for witnesses, protective measures which are ordinarily the prohibition for all parties to disclose these documents to the press. The Chamber is very aware of those measures. In order to save some time, would the Trial Chamber like us to make the request orally, and then we can do it today? Or would the Trial Chamber prefer to rule on the basis of a written submission? I put myself in your hands for that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Terrier, I think perhaps you could develop it now orally, and then I can see with my colleagues whether or not we're going to deal with the issue orally or if it needs to be in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecution's concern is the following: We're going to disclose to the Defence a certain number of witness statements as part of the case files on the incidents that I have already spoken about and as part of the general obligation for disclosure, provided for under Rule 66. What we would like, and of course I'm not criticising the Defence in any way, but in all cases which have been dealt with in this Tribunal, I believe, or at least most of them, it must be clearly indicated by the Judges that the Defence must not disclose to third parties who are not authorised to communicate those witness statements, or to the media. And it should be made clear that if the Defence intends to contact some of the witnesses whose names we have identified to it, it not -- if necessary, the Trial Chamber -- the witnesses, they should be so informed in advance so that the witnesses, if necessary, would be defended by somebody from the OTP, and that would be a reciprocal arrangement; so that when we are given names by the Defence, we would not be in contact with those witnesses unless we have first notified that we are doing so to the Defence. These are classical, traditional measures that the Tribunal has already granted in other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, do you have any objections to that request, the request that the Prosecutor has just made, or do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I'm clear on what he's asking for. I understand that if witness statements and names are given to the Defence that the Defence would not give the same to the press. I don't have a problem with that, if that's what he's asking. I find it a little unusual, because they choose to have a Rule 61 in open hearing, where the whole world, including the media, listen to these witnesses. But nevertheless, I certainly can live with an order which would not give those statements or the names of those witnesses to the press. So if that's what he's asking for, I don't have a problem. As far as contacting those witnesses, I'm not sure what -- and maybe I'm not picking up the interpretation well enough. I oftentimes like to have an investigator, or personally with an investigator, to speak to a perspective witness, if that witness would speak to me, obviously. It's their choice, I guess. And if they would like to know ahead of time that I wish to speak with that witness, I don't have that problem. So I'm not sure if I've covered everything that they want, but that's my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Terrier, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I want to explain the Prosecution's position to Mr. Kostic. What we want are three things, I'll be very brief, and I'm going to add a fourth. First, the Defence must not disclose to third parties, who are not authorised -- that is, individuals who are not part of the Defence team, who are not counsel, chosen by General Galic, who are not investigators chosen by the Defence team -- the names of the witnesses, the addresses of the witnesses, or the substance of their statements. This must remain within the Defence team, only among those people who are authorised to defend the accused General Galic. That was the first measure. The second is that we want the Defence not to disclose to the media the names, addresses of the witnesses, and the substance of their statements. And Mr. Kostic said that that did not present any problems to him. The third measure that we're asking for is that the Defence not be in contact with any witness which is designated by the Prosecution without our being first informed of that step; so that we, if necessary, if that's the witness' wish, can be present at the meeting. That measure, of course, is a reciprocal one. The final measure, perhaps this is just a recall, is that were it to happen that Mr. Kostic or another counsel were to withdraw from the Defence of General Galic, a time period be allowed so that the documents given to him be given back to the Prosecution. I think that's a basic issue. These are the three or four measures that we are asking the Tribunal to order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, have you understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think Mr. Terrier --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier talked about four requests. I don't have a problem -- I think we can certainly honour the first, the second, and the third. In regard to the fourth, I think that my duty, at least under the canons of ethics under which I practise, that if I withdraw from a case, the file goes to my successor, as opposed to the Prosecution. So I'm telling the Court that that is a potential issue, and I think that I certainly have no problem turning the file over to my successor. So that's not a problem. With that modification, I do not have a problem with the requests of Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fortunately, the Chamber is here, the full Chamber, and the decision is to grant the request of the Prosecution so that we can move quickly in respect of the documents, but the Chamber -- well, this is an oral decision, and the general terms are that we are going to grant the request of the Prosecutor. But so that things remain very clear, we are going to rendered a written decision. So as regards the objective of starting our work, you have the decision, and subsequently we will rendered a written decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Wald has just drawn my attention to a particular aspect. Mr. Kostic did not agree on the point of the request having to do with giving back the documents to the Prosecutor, but felt that they should be given back to his successor. I don't know whether Mr. Terrier wants to say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would go back to what you have just said. It seems to me that it might be more in compliance with the Rules, in light of our disclosure obligations, for Mr. Kostic, if that were to happen -- perhaps it won't happen -- that he were to give us back the documents and we would give them to his successor. If the Chamber prefers that -- well, I know that the legal practice in many countries is different. But if the Chamber wants us to proceed differently, we will do so. I simply rely on the discretion of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we all agree on the first three points, and that's been decided.
